tldr: We propose S², a novel metric that measures how geometrically well an embodied foundation model's sensory representation (images and text) aligns with physical motion trajectories. It correlates strongly and positively with task success rates in both simulation and real-world robots, enabling the identification of promising models offline before costly real-robot rollouts or fine-tuning.
hero_caption: Core concept and representative results of this work. Left: Based on the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), the representation spaces of sensory observations (vision and language) and motor execution (trajectories) should align. Right: Across 12 VLA models, the proposed metric S² shows a strong correlation (r = +0.717) with success rates in SimplerEnv.
overview:
When evaluating robotic foundation models, closed-loop evaluation—intervening in real environments or simulators to verify success—is extremely slow, expensive, and a major bottleneck. Conventional offline evaluations have relied on visual question answering (VQA) scores for VLMs (vision-language models) or image quality metrics (like FID) for video generation models. However, these only measure passive recognition or visual appearance. They fail to capture whether representations are optimized for robot action. Visually similar scenes may require completely different motions, while visually distinct scenes might call for the exact same action.

To tackle this, the authors extend the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH)—which posits that representations converge toward a shared statistical model of reality as modalities scale—to robotics. Treating a robot's physical motion trajectory as another modality projecting the real world, they hypothesized that more capable embodied models should have sensory representations (vision and language) that align geometrically with physical motion representations. This insight led to Sensorimotor Alignment (S²), a training-free offline metric.

Empirical evaluations demonstrate that S² correlates strongly and positively with downstream task success across VLAs (vision-language-action models), WAMs (world action models), and even real-world robot policies. While VQA scores and visual quality metrics show little to no correlation with success rates, S² accurately pinpoints promising models tied directly to action. Furthermore, it serves as a powerful diagnostic tool, uncovering internal representation-level mechanisms behind puzzling phenomena such as why VLAs often ignore text instructions and rely solely on visual cues.
contributions: Extended the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) to robotics, presenting a new perspective that capable embodied models geometrically align sensory representations with motor representations.
Developed S², a lightweight, training-free offline metric that computes the neighborhood overlap between sensory and motor spaces.
Demonstrated that S² correlates strongly with downstream task success rates (r ≈ 0.7 to 0.8) across diverse model families including VLAs, raw unadapted VLMs, WAMs, and real-world robots.
Used S² to explain model behaviors at the representation level, such as visual dominance in VLAs (ignoring instructions) and performance drops when freezing the vision encoder.

sections.heading: Goodbye Costly Real-Robot Rollouts? Predicting Robot Success via Representation Alignment
sections.summary: Because evaluating robotic foundation models is prohibitively expensive, cheap offline proxies are urgently needed. Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, this paper proposes S², a metric measuring the geometric alignment between sensory representations and motion trajectories, showing that it reliably predicts downstream task success.
sections.details:
Robotics is experiencing rapid advances powered by foundation models built on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generation models. However, selecting the best model typically demands closed-loop rollouts on real robots or in simulators. This incurs massive hardware and time costs, creating a major headache for researchers.

One convenient alternative has been using offline proxies like VQA accuracy for VLMs or pixel-level metrics (such as FID and SSIM) for generated videos. Yet these merely measure passive recognition or visual fidelity. They do not reflect whether the representation is suited for action. To succeed at a manipulation task, a robot must generate distinct trajectories even in visually similar scenes. Sensory representations must be fundamentally tied to motor execution.

Here, the authors look to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH). PRH suggests that as models across different modalities (images, text) scale, their representations converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. The authors asked: could robot motion trajectories be another projection modality of the physical world? In other words, as embodied models become more capable, their sensory representations should cleanly align with the geometry of physical motion.

To test this hypothesis, they developed Sensorimotor Alignment (S²), a training-free offline metric. S² not only correlates strongly with downstream robot task success rates, but also acts as a diagnostic lens to explain previously opaque model behaviors from an internal representation perspective.

sections.heading: Comparing Sensory and Motor Neighbors: How S² Is Computed
sections.summary: S² evaluates how well neighborhood episodes overlap between sensory space (images and text) and motor space (end-effector trajectories) on a reference dataset. Requiring no training, it measures geometric alignment by combining cosine distance with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW).
sections.details:
The mechanism behind S² is intuitive and elegant. If situations that look similar to a model also correspond to situations where the robot moves similarly, the model possesses an internal representation well-suited for embodiment. The concrete steps are as follows:

- Preparing the Reference Dataset:
Sample $N$ episodes from a robot manipulation dataset (such as DROID or BridgeDataV2). For each episode $i$, sample a single image frame and the task instruction as sensory input $\mathbf{x}_i$.

- Extracting Sensory Representations:
Feed the sensory input into the robot foundation model's vision and text encoders, then average-pool the resulting token features into a $d$-dimensional embedding vector $\mathbf{z}_i$.

- Constructing Motor Representations:
Extract the end-effector position $(x,y,z)$, orientation angles $(\phi,\theta,\psi)$, and gripper state $g$ across a future horizon of $h$ steps following the sampled frame. Positions live in 3D Euclidean space, while rotations respect the geometric structure of the 3D rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$.

- Calculating Neighborhood Alignment:
In sensory space, find the $k$-nearest neighbors (the most similar episodes) for each query using the cosine distance of the embeddings. In motor space, compute trajectory distances using Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to account for variations in execution speed, and retrieve the $k$-nearest motor neighbors.

Finally, calculate the fraction of shared episodes between the sensory neighborhood set and the motor neighborhood set, averaging across all episodes. A higher overlap yields a larger S² value, indicating that sensory and motor spaces are beautifully aligned.

captions.F2: Illustration of the S² measurement procedure. For a query episode (left), nearest neighbors are retrieved in both sensory space (bottom right) and motion trajectory space (top right). A higher count of shared episodes appearing in both neighborhood sets (green checkmarks) indicates stronger sensorimotor alignment.

sections.heading: Can Representations Predict Success? Strong Correlations in Sim and Real Robots
sections.summary: Across 12 VLAs, 8 unadapted VLMs, 6 WAMs, and real-world robot policies, S² exhibits strong positive correlations with task success. Where conventional VQA scores and video metrics fail, S² accurately predicts performance differences.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Validating Correlations Across Model Families
The authors rigorously tested the relationship between S² and actual task success across diverse model families.
- VLA Models: Evaluating 12 VLAs in the SimplerEnv simulator yielded a Pearson correlation of $r = +0.717$, demonstrating a very strong relationship. Models with higher alignment consistently achieve higher success rates on downstream manipulation tasks.
- Unadapted Raw VLMs: Computing S² on 8 off-the-shelf VLMs before fine-tuning them on robot data correlated at $r = +0.681$ ($p = 0.031$) with their eventual success rates once trained into VLAs. This means researchers can scout the best VLM backbones before investing in expensive fine-tuning.
- World Action Models (WAMs): Across 6 video-generation-based WAMs (on the ALOHA dataset and RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark), S² also correlated strongly at $r = +0.718$.
- Real-World Robots: For 5 public MolmoB0T checkpoints evaluated under a unified protocol on real DROID hardware across 40 tasks, S² achieved an impressive correlation of $r = +0.831$ ($p = 0.041$).

### 3.2 Comparison with Existing Offline Proxies
Compared to conventional passive metrics, S²'s advantage is striking. Overall VQA benchmark scores for unadapted VLMs showed virtually no correlation with VLA success ($r = -0.154$, slightly negative). For WAMs, standard video metrics fell short (SSIM at $r = +0.558$, PSNR at $r = +0.468$, and FID inversely correlated at $r = +0.680$, where worse video quality bizarrely implied higher success). In contrast, S² predicted success with near-perfect accuracy at $r = +0.999$.

### 3.3 Robustness and Negative Controls
The positive correlation held consistently across variations in neighborhood size $k$, horizon length $h$, reference datasets (DROID vs. BridgeDataV2), and metric weighting. As a negative control, the authors introduced an embodiment mismatch by evaluating a bimanual WAM against single-arm robot data (DROID). The correlation plummeted from $r = +0.999$ down to $r = +0.246$. This proves S² is not capturing statistical noise, but rather the robot's true physical morphology.

sections.heading: Why Does That Happen? Explaining Internal Model Dynamics with S²
sections.summary: Behaviors previously observed only through empirical closed-loop trial and error—such as ignoring language instructions or performance drops from frozen encoders—can now be explained at the representation level using S².
sections.details:
S² is more than a performance predictor; it serves as a powerful lens for diagnosing internal model mechanisms. The authors clarified four mysteries documented in prior work.

### 4.1 Modality Dominance: Why VLAs Ignore Text Instructions
Prior studies observed that VLAs often suffer from weak instruction grounding, relying primarily on visual appearance rather than language commands. When decomposing output tokens into visual, text, and joint representations, fine-tuned VLAs showed that only visual feature S² correlated with success ($r = +0.694$), while text feature S² had negligible correlation ($r = +0.237$). This provides representation-level proof that fine-tuned VLAs lean excessively on visual representations when generating actions, failing to link language to motor execution.

### 4.2 Performance Drops from Freezing Vision Encoders
Freezing a VLM's vision encoder during fine-tuning is known to degrade VLA performance. Experiments revealed that freezing the encoder caused a 41% drop in S² and a corresponding 40% drop in success rate. End-to-end fine-tuning succeeds precisely because it actively pulls sensory representations closer to the geometry of physical motion.

### 4.3 Why Early Diffusion Steps Determine Action
In video-diffusion-based WAMs, recent work showed actions can be decoded directly from early latent states without completing the full iterative denoising process. Tracking S² across denoising steps revealed that S² reached near-peak values by the very first step, fluctuating by only about 6% across remaining steps. Because motor alignment is established so early, models can skip downstream video generation and still succeed at the task.

### 4.4 Middle Layers Align Most Strongly with Motion
While intermediate layers of video diffusion models are known to capture semantic concepts, analyzing a 30-block WAM revealed a distinct peak in S² at Block 14. The exact layers responsible for semantic reasoning resonate most strongly with physical robot actions.

sections.heading: Robot Representation Learning and the Platonic Hypothesis: Contextualizing This Work
sections.summary: Prior work focused on evaluating static properties of isolated vision encoders without incorporating physical robot motion trajectories. This paper bridges the Platonic Representation Hypothesis to the action modality for the first time, achieving action-grounded representation evaluation.
sections.details:
Representation learning in robotics has long debated how to evaluate pretrained vision encoders. Previous attempts investigated properties like segmentation capability or feature norm entropy. However, these metrics were often restricted to specific architectures or saw their correlations break down depending on the downstream policy learning algorithm. Crucially, none incorporated the actual physical trajectories executed by the robot into the evaluation criteria.

Meanwhile, in foundational AI theory, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) gained traction across image generation, video diffusion, and multimodal LLMs. Yet these studies remained confined to observational data like images and text. This work bridges PRH with robotics for the first time by treating physical robot trajectories as another projection modality of reality.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Looking Ahead: Toward Directly Optimizing Alignment
sections.summary: Sensorimotor Alignment (S²) provides a low-cost, accurate offline evaluation proxy and a versatile diagnostic tool. Beyond observing correlations, future work points toward directly optimizing S² as a training loss.
sections.details:
This paper introduced S², a metric measuring the geometric alignment between an embodied model's sensory representations and its end-effector trajectories. S² strongly correlates with task success across VLAs, raw VLMs, WAMs, and real-robot policies, substantially outperforming conventional VQA and video quality metrics as an offline proxy. It also offers concrete representation-level explanations for internal model dynamics.

While this study primarily utilizes S² for model selection and diagnosis, the finding that higher sensorimotor alignment yields higher success points to an exciting next step: directly optimizing S² during training by introducing regularization or loss functions that explicitly align sensory representations with motion trajectories.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Rigorous Robustness Checks
sections.summary: The appendix details dataset sampling protocols, DTW distance definitions accounting for SO(3) rotations, and controlled experiments eliminating confounding factors such as architecture or training recipes.
sections.details:
The appendix outlines essential engineering choices and detailed experimental controls supporting the paper's claims.

- Datasets and Sampling:
Single-arm experiments utilize DROID (Franka Panda, 15Hz) and BridgeDataV2 (WidowX, 5Hz), while bimanual experiments employ ALOHA (14 DoF). To ensure fair comparisons across horizons $h$, fixed anchor frames were sampled once using the maximum horizon $H_{\max}$ (220 for DROID, 40 for Bridge), and shorter horizons simply truncated these trajectories.

- Local Cost and DTW:
In addition to Euclidean distance for end-effector position, orientation distance is computed as an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ geodesic distance using quaternions, combined with gripper state differences to define a local step cost. Accumulating this via Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) provides a trajectory distance robust to variations in execution speed.

- Controlled Experiments for Confounders:
The authors verified that VLA correlations were not artifacts of confounding variables like model size or training data. Correlations held strong among unadapted VLMs trained under identical recipes ($r = +0.681$), and leave-one-out tests systematically removing individual model families consistently preserved positive correlations.

takeaways: Embodied models should not be evaluated with passive VQA scores or visual image quality, but by measuring whether their sensory representations geometrically align with physical motion trajectories (S²).
S² enables identifying promising foundation backbones offline before deploying on real robots/simulators, and even before fine-tuning VLMs on robot data.
The reason VLAs tend to ignore language instructions is that fine-tuning predominantly aligns visual features with motion, leaving text representations unaligned.
Beyond serving as a low-cost model selection proxy, S² represents a promising candidate objective function to maximize directly during policy training.
limitations: This work demonstrates a strong correlation between S² and task success, but has not yet proven causality—whether directly optimizing S² during training directly boosts policy success remains to be established.

Because models with similar S² scores can occasionally exhibit variance in success rates, S² serves best as a pre-filtering prioritization tool rather than a total replacement for closed-loop evaluations.

The evaluated model families, benchmark environments, and real-world experiments remain limited in scope, leaving generalizability across diverse manipulation domains and mobile robots as future work.
